Depth changes by factor ~15 between sectors with high significance, which for a planet should be steady up to calibration. sector_depths_by_source verdict changes_within_a_source with TESS-SPOC p_constant 6.4922611315343275e-15 confirms astrophysical/depth or dilution change, not just aperture.
Significant odd/even depth difference strongly favours an eclipsing binary folded at half its true period (or two different dips), not a single planet period 6.69 and 13.4.

This spot-to-sector change within the same light-curve product and same pipeline, combined with a 3/few-percent distance-dependent modulation, positively favors systematics/blend/variability over a single stable transiting planet on the target.

Depth is highly inconsistent: 10258 ppm (sector 42), 5080 ppm (sector 57), 24102 ppm (sector 70), 13822 ppm (sector 84) with chi2 32.24 dof 3. sector_depths_by_source verdict changes_within_a_source (QLP p_constant 0.018, TESS-SPOC p_constant 1.885869328204775e-05) and transit_depths p_consistent 2.900319570266961e-10 with chi2 56.00786758296972 dof 6, share_of_top_3 0.806. Planet size alone (3.112 Rearth) and flat shape are not diagnostic — a small star's grazing eclipse and a blended binary's eclipses can both be flat-bottomed with no secondary or odd/even difference. The low ML rank and the large depth scatter outweigh these mild planet-like flags.
Significant second dip well above brightening indicates a stellar eclipse of ~19% dip depth, inconsistent with a planet; hot Jupiter occultation would be much smaller.
Large out-of-eclipse modulation at this period points to ellipsoidal/reflected light from a close binary, not a planet.
Depth changes by ~79% between sectors, as expected for a blended/NEB eclipse with different apertures, not a planet.

The dip period is exactly one times the spot rotation period with huge variability (~8e4 ppm). Phase_curve amplitude 996.1 ppm ratio_to_depth 0.2035 chi2 53.03/9 and sector_depths_by_source changes confirm variability dominates. Dip at rotation multiple with this swing favours spots, not a planet.
Transit is far too long for tic_radius 0.779881 R_sun and does not match stellar density; density mismatch plus light-curve variability together rule out a planet transit.

Strong odd/even depth difference (5.822 sigma, 80.96% difference) is classic for an eclipsing binary at twice the reported period (22.8 d). Odd transits are ~5.3x deeper than even, opposite parity as expected for primary+secondary eclipses.

Individual transit depths are wildly inconsistent, with one or two very deep events (3595, 3587, 2810 ppm) dominating the signal (95.7% of SNR) and several flat/shallow (29, -146 ppm) inconsistent with a planet of fixed depth. Not explained by calibration alone.

Depth appears to change dramatically between sectors and data sources, and the planet classifier ranks this as much less planet-like than the median known planet (0.07). Combined with the odd/even evidence this points to stellar variability, systematics and/or a close binary/bblend rather than a steady planet; flat-bottom shape (v_sigma=-2.273) and small size (rp_rearth=1.999) alone do not overcome this.
Flat bottom (negative V score) and ingress fraction 0.1 favour a transit over a grazing binary/V shape.
With rp/rstar 0.0532 the implied radius is planet-sized well below the 10 Rearth threshold, not stellar.
Duration 3.5h vs central 2.434h is up to 1.5x, fit at b=0.8102 — consistent with an eccentric/high impact-parameter small-planet transit.

Depth changes by factors well beyond errors even within one source; not a calibration offset, as SPOC 2-min alone varies from 542 to 7225 ppm. A true planet on target should be steady regardless of aperture/processing.

Individual transits are wildly inconsistent, with one or two deep events carrying the entire detection and others consistent with no transit or even negative depth. Signal strength is driven by outliers, classic for a blend/false alarm.
Independent classifier trained on solved TESS candidates ranks this in the bottom 5% of planet-like signals, consistent with the observed instability.

Odd and even dips differ by ~9.7 sigma (ratio 3.7). Sector-level odd/even also extreme (sector_oe_max_sigma=8.587). This is the classic signature of an eclipsing binary at twice the reported period, not a planet.

Depth does not repeat even within the same SPOC 2-min source. One transit (sector 27, epoch -1) is 13±242 ppm (i.e. absent) while others are 3499, 364, 2928 ppm. High share on top 3 and extreme chi2 show a few bad events, consistent with a blended or eccentric EB, not a stable planet.

Observed duration 3.499 h is much longer than central 2.242 h for this M-dwarf (rad 0.3545), implying a very eccentric or misaligned binary grazing geometry. Flat bottom favours full eclipses, not grazing.

Planet-sized, sub-Saturn dip observed longer than central but still fits a M-dwarf transit (≈1.3× central with Gaia radii) with stellar-density consistent shape (fit chi2_red 1.49, b≈0) and no V-shape (v_sigma 2.641 <3).
No odd/even difference and no significant secondary at half orbit (secondary below threshold and phase not 0.5); period-doubled EB ruled out despite xgboost planet_rank 0.06.

No nearby star inside one TESS pixel (21 arcsec) that can produce 5000 ppm even with deep eclipse, and depth is steady within source and between the two individual transits per light curve, ruling out a blended neighbour EB or aperture / few-bad-transit noise (refit snr 17.75) — inconclusive centroid is not off-target evidence.

Odd and even transits differ by ~1500 ppm at 4.976 sigma, with 2.3x depth ratio and same sign in all sectors (sector_oe_max_sigma=6.924, sector_oe_sectors_over_3=1, sector_oe_same_sign_share=1). Strong positive evidence for an eclipsing binary at twice the 13.9 d period rather than a planet.

Individual transit depths are wildly inconsistent, with one transit essentially flat (-38 ppm) and another much deeper (2627 ppm), carrying 98.5% of the signal. Shape is not a planet; the 'transits' are a few bad events, not a consistent planet signal.

Star is highly spotted variable with strong rotation signal; combined with highly variable depths and low SNX (xgboost planet_rank=0.09) this favours variability / spot systematics and EB over an unvarying planet, despite flat shape (v_sigma=-4.079) and planet radius (rp_rearth=2.176).

Significant alternating odd/even depth difference persists in the same sign across sectors is the positive signature of an eclipsing binary folded at twice the reported period (period_x2 29.6 d), not a planetary transit with stable depth.

Large brightness swing at this period outside the dips, chi2 much above unity and larger than any secondary eclipse, indicates ellipsoidal/spot modulation from a close stellar companion rather than a planet.
Only three transits all near a gap carry the whole signal, increasing the false-alarm rate for variability and making the odd/even and phase-curve signatures harder to dismiss as noise.

Even and odd eclipses have essentially no odd depth and a ~630 ppm even depth; sigma >3 with real depth difference, plus sector_oe_max_sigma 6.723 in 6 of 39 sectors with same sign, is the classic signature of an eclipsing binary at double the detected period (period_x2 23.2) folded as single at 11.6 d.

Depth changes significantly within the same light-curve product, not a calibration offset, inconsistent with a planet on the target and expected when secondary eclipses of an EB are folded at half the true period.

Depth changes by a factor ~2 within the same SPOC 2-min product and even flips sign; transit_depths verdict changes_within_a_source with 2 outliers >4 sigma. A real planet on a 14.7 d period should be steady within a single product, so this is not a planet transit but spot/crowding systematics or a few bad events dominating the fit.
Independent classifier rates this as strongly planet-unlike, consistent with the measured depth instability.

A star within 1 TESS pixel (21 arcsec) can produce the folded 3178 ppm dip with a <25% eclipse and centroid has no clear offset to test it, keeping a blended EB viable, though depth variability still positively favors non-planet systematics over a single EB.
Depth is highly inconsistent between sectors - positive in two sectors, near-zero or negative in others - inconsistent with a planet on the target.
Depth changes significantly within the same pipeline (SPOC 2-min: 557 ppm in sector 19 vs 32 ppm in sector 25 vs -62 ppm in sector 53, etc.), not a calibration difference between products.
Signal dominated by two extremely deep dips and one missing dip, indicating a planet-sized depth only when two individual events drive the detection; not a consistent transiting planet.
Four transits do not share a consistent depth; one is completely absent, meaning the signal is not a repeated transit with stable depth.
Depth changes by sector and is near zero in sector 58, which a planet on the target must not do; sector_depths_by_source verdict changes_within_a_source confirms it is not a calibration offset.
All detected transits fall near data gaps, a false-alarm signature, not a regular planet ephemeris.
Large out-of-transit swing at this period (32% of dip depth) points to spots/system variability, not a quiet planet transit.
Star is strongly variable at 5.7-15 d, comparable to the 13.1 d dip. Phase curve and rotation together favour variability as the source of the dip rather than a planet.

Depth changes significantly between sectors (flat depth disfavoured, p << 0.01) and sector_depths_by_source says changes_within_a_source (TESS-SPOC p_constant 1.4451656295605937e-05). True planets are steady; this variability is more like spot modulation or blended contamination.
Odd depth 209.8 ppm vs even 1135 ppm, depth_difference 0.8152 (925.6 ppm) with ratio 5.4. Strong odd/even difference indicates binary at twice the period (27.8 d), not a planet.
Depth changes between sectors in the same light-curve product; 15% mean drop in sector 1 and 8% in sector 2 vs 5574 ppm in sector 13 and 2540 ppm in sector 87. Not a calibration difference.
Signal not reproducible: top three events carry 0.931 of total signal, many depths negative/upper-limit. Two shallow transits in sectors 1-2 when eclipse is deep in sectors 13, 87, 94.
Depth changes by factor ~3.5 across sectors (108 to 754 ppm) with chi2 150.9 dof 11, inconsistent with a planet of fixed depth.
Depth changes significantly even within the same light-curve product, so the variation is astrophysical/calibration, not a change between pipelines.

Odd and even dips look different at ~2.85 sigma as part of pattern that repeats with sign changes (sector_oe_max_sigma 7.739, 5 sectors >3 sigma), favouring a binary at twice the period over a planet.

Depths are wildly inconsistent, chi2/dof 187.28/15, driven by three very deep transits that carry 87% of the folded signal; false-alarm signature of a few outlier events, consistent with sector_depths_by_source showing QLP 237±97 ppm vs TESS-SPOC 2114±181 ppm (differs_by_source, p_constant 2.797e-18).
Apparent depth change is between light-curve products/catalogues, not astrophysical sectors within a source; supports software artefact rather than a stable planet transit.

Difference images give no on-target confirmation; centroid_all not run, so cannot rule out a diluted NEB, but size is planet-like (rp_rearth 1.249, duration ratio 1.303, shape v_sigma 1.479) and identical centroid limitation applies to many false alarms in similar set (2/5 not a planet). xgboost planet_rank 0.1 also favours false positive.
Depth changes dramatically between sectors, from 1586 +/-163 ppm in sector 24 to 33 +/-70 ppm in sector 51, not consistent with a planet on the target.
Depth varies significantly even within the same light-curve product (SPOC 2-min p_constant 2.382788474052658e-10), so it cannot be a calibration offset between products.
Only a few outliers drive the entire signal; most transits are undetected, indicating noise/false alarm rather than repeated planet transits.

A secondary dip near phase 0.756 with SNR above 5 and comparable to the brightest brightening suggests a stellar eclipse (phase offset from 0.5 for eccentric EB), not a planet. Combined with sec_half_max_snr 5.331 shows it persists at half period.

Sector-level odd/even differences exceed 3 sigma in one sector, consistent with a binary at twice the detected period (21 d) with unequal primary and secondary eclipses. Sector_oe_same_sign_share 0.6667 shows not a single bright-spot outlier.

Individual transit depths vary by >10 sigma with the top 3 transits carrying 92.6% of signal. This is not sector-level dilution but astrophysical depth change/flattening expected for an eccentric EB folded at half its true period.

Odd (828.8 ppm) and even (496.7 ppm) depths differ by 40%, depth_ratio 1.7; not a statistical fluctuation, favours an eclipsing binary at twice the 10.5 d period or residual systematics at high significance.

sec tool shows depth changes_within_a_source: SPOC 2-min p_constant 2.4229101895258697e-62 with per-sector depths 1847±273, 407±209, 3168±129, -95±163 ppm; TESS-SPOC gives ~0 ppm. A real planet on the target must be stable; such extremes by aperture alone only point to systematics/stellar variability masquerading as an unstable folded dip.

Grazing V-shaped geometry with impact parameter near unity and fit_log_density_ratio -2.07 / star_density_penalty 62.75, inconsistent with a central planet transit despite v_sigma 0.5468; better matches a near-grazing blended binary.
54 transits should agree if they are a planet, but chi2=728.2334745858368 dof=53 shows extreme scatter; individual depths range ~ -1009 to 4206 ppm.
Following Tool transit_depths, the signal is dominated by a few outliers (3872, 3362, 4206 ppm), the classic signature of a few bad events / spot crossings rather than coherent transits.

Depths change drastically and unpredictably between sectors; sector_depths_by_source confirms changes_within_a_source with p_constant=2.8569565190800305e-74 for SPOC 2-min alone, not a calibration offset.
Odd and even transits have a 75% depth difference at ~5.8 sigma - expected for an eclipsing binary folded at half its true period. At this bright Tmag=9.594 significant difference is astrophysical
A real secondary eclipse is present well outside the detrending bump (depth ~46% of the primary), inconsistent with a planet and indicating a luminous companion
Depth is not stable - consistent with blending/detrending artefacts. sector_depths_by_source verdict=changes_within_a_source confirms true depth changes versus a planet
Flat-bottomed (not V-shaped) favours planet over grazing binary; sector_oe_max_sigma 1.186 and sector_oe_sectors_over_3 0

Odd/even difference below 4 sigma and not sustained in sectors; could be noise in 3 transits rather than true binary at 27.4 d, with secondary at 0.5156 phase having snr 5.584 and best_brightening_snr 4.225 (ratio 1.322) not well above noise

No off-target detection; neighbours.plausible_within_1px 0 and could_cause_within_1px 0, so no nearby star can produce 1121 ppm dip with <=25% eclipse, ruling out neighbour blend despite inconclusive centroid
odd and even transits differ by ~47% at ~3 sigma, with sector_oe_max_sigma 4.15, favouring an eclipsing binary at twice the period over a planet. A planet would have consistent odd/even depths.

A strong secondary dip near ~0.76 phase, 31% as deep as the primary, significantly above the best brightening, indicates stellar pulsations/eclipses from a blended or bound binary rather than a planet (hot-Jupiter tiny secondary not seen at this depth for rp_rearth 0.7984).

Individual transit depths are highly inconsistent; one outlier carries nearly half the signal, consistent with a few bad or diluted eclipses, not a stable planetary transit. Sector depths also appear different (sectors.p_constant 0.001964) but sector_depths_by_source says differs_by_source not changes_within_a_source, supporting calibration offsets amplifying the outlier, but planet case remains excluded.
Depth changes by 307.9% across 5 sectors (chi2 109.1, dof 4) — not stable even within one pipeline.

SPOC 2-min depths are 1545±236 ppm (sector 23), -141±112 ppm (sector 49) and 1254±129 ppm (sector 50): formally negative in one sector and ~10x deeper in others, proving pipeline-independent variation.
High share indicates a few deep events carry the signal, not a consistent small dip; consistent with noise/GBS variability dominating the 3.998-h window.

Dip period equals star's spot period (1.003x) with huge spot modulation (up to 35499 ppm) in sector 64, and phase_curve amplitude 281.2 ppm ratio_to_depth 0.4597 chi2 70.21 dof9; stellar variability, not a planet, is the best explanation
Depth changes actually within the same pipeline across sectors for a sector with 11-44 transits at SNR 29.48; noise from spots/pipeline changes mimics transits, opposite of stable planet
2.99h dip far too long for a central planet around this M dwarf (0.6547 Rsun 0.6306 Msun) and implies grazing; flat shape v_sigma=-2.785 alone not diagnostic for flat-bottom planet

Strong odd/even difference (6 sigma) with 2.3x deeper even dips and sector_oe_max_sigma 11.73 and 2 sectors over 3 same sign 0.8 suggests binary at twice the reported period (27.8 d), not alternating planet transits.
Depth changes by factor >10 between sectors and verdict changes_within_a_source (TESS-SPOC p_constant 5.533e-81). Single-sector detection at 2977 ppm cannot be a stable planet.
Signal is driven by 3 extreme outlier transits (97% of signal). With chi2 704.8/10 and 5.6e-145 consistency, dips are not consistent repeats of one transit depth.

Depths are not consistent: top 3 transits carry share_of_top_3 0.982 of the signal with depths 2703 ppm (8.4 sigma) and 2046 ppm (6.3 sigma) vs. mean 775 ppm and one non-detection -43 ppm, chi2 184.60676126798336 dof 9.

Depth changes drastically between sectors (depth_change_pct 314.3); sector_depths_by_source verdict changes_within_a_source with SPOC 2-min p_constant 7.128097778397709e-11, depths 28 ppm (sector 24) vs 1551 ppm (sector 25) vs 1001 ppm (sector 52) proving variability not pipeline calibration.

Odd (631.3 ppm) vs even (1190 ppm) depth difference 0.4695 (558.8 ppm) ratio 1.9; sector_oe_max_sigma 5.076 in 1 sector over 3, indicating odd/even inconsistency on target, not a stable planet at 11.9 d.
Odd and even dips differ by >8 sigma with ratio 2.2, best explained by an eclipsing binary at twice the 14.5 d period (29 d) rather than a planet at 14.5 d with alternating primary/secondary.

Five transits are extremely inconsistent; two are missing/shallow at ~223-97 ppm and two are twice as deep at ~1137-964 ppm, so signal is carried by a few anomalous events, not a planet folding consistently.

Depth changes dramatically between sectors (by >2x) with p_constant 1.545e-25, and sector_depths_by_source verdict changes_within_a_source confirms real astrophysical change, inconsistent with a stable planetary transit while supporting a blended or active binary scenario.
Depth is not stable; the variation is far larger than measurement errors, so the signal is not a repeated transit of constant depth.

Variation persists within the same light-curve product (QLP) between sectors — not a calibration difference between products. The earliest SPOC sector shows essentially no dip, ruling out a planet with steady depth.
Individual transit depths are highly inconsistent; a few outliers are tens of times the mean, which drives the overall detection instead of a consistent transit.
